title: Bending Light: Reflection & Refraction
summary: Bend mirrors and lenses by hand to discover how reflection, refraction, and total internal reflection actually work.
theory: Light travels in straight lines until it meets a new surface, where it obeys one of two rules. **Reflection**: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; curving the mirror (concave) gathers parallel rays to a single **principal focus (F)**, related to the radius of curvature by f = R/2. **Refraction**: light changes speed crossing between media, bending its path according to Snell's Law, n = sin i / sin r. A convex lens uses this to focus light to a point whose position depends on the object distance u relative to f (1/v − 1/u = 1/f). When light inside a denser medium hits a boundary steeper than the **critical angle** (sin θc = 1/n), it undergoes **total internal reflection** and cannot escape at all — the principle behind optical fibres.

procedure.title: Bend the concave mirror
procedure.description: Drag the glowing ring on the mirror's rim to change its curvature and watch the focal point F move.

procedure.title: Find the burning point
procedure.description: Slide the paper screen until it sits exactly at F and observe what happens; then switch to bulb mode and place the bulb at F to produce a parallel beam.

procedure.title: Squash the convex lens
procedure.description: Drag the candle and the lens, and use the bulge handle to change the lens's focal length. Note how the image changes from real & inverted to virtual & magnified as the candle crosses F.

procedure.title: Find the critical angle
procedure.description: Drag the torch inside the glass/water/diamond block and sweep the angle until the beam suddenly stops escaping — that is the critical angle, and beyond it you get total internal reflection.

procedure.title: Build an instrument
procedure.description: On the optician's bench, arrange the two lenses and the object to complete each mission: a telescope, a microscope, and a projector.

observation: The mirror's focal length shortens as its curvature deepens, matching f = R/2. The lens image flips from real/inverted to virtual/magnified exactly when the object crosses the focal point. Total internal reflection begins abruptly once the incidence angle passes the critical angle predicted by sin θc = 1/n, with denser media (diamond) showing a much smaller critical angle than water or glass.

quiz.question: Bending a concave mirror to a deeper curve (smaller radius of curvature) will:

options.text: Move the focal point farther away
Move the focal point closer to the mirror

quiz.explanation: Since f = R/2, a smaller radius of curvature R produces a shorter focal length f, pulling the focus closer to the mirror.

quiz.question: A candle placed exactly at a convex lens's focal point produces:

options.text: No image — the outgoing rays are parallel

quiz.explanation: At u = f, the lens equation gives v = infinity: every ray leaves the lens parallel to the axis, so no image forms.

quiz.question: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels:

options.text: From a denser medium into a rarer medium, above the critical angle
From a rarer medium into a denser medium, at any angle

quiz.explanation: TIR requires light moving from higher to lower refractive index, and only once the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle sin θc = 1/n.

title: Panamá Canal: Lock & Lift System
summary: Explore the physics of the Panama Canal lock system using gravity, buoyancy, and hydrostatic pressure to move ships.
theory: The Panamá Canal lock staircase uses a series of water-filled chambers and miter gates to lift ships from sea level to Gatún Lake. Gravity flow valves move water between chambers—no pumps are required. A ship's buoyancy and hydrostatic pressure equalize the water levels, allowing safe transit across the continental divide.

procedure.title: Execute Step
procedure.description: Progress through the 13-step sequence to see how water is moved to change the ship's elevation.

procedure.title: Monitor Live Readouts
procedure.description: Observe the ship elevation, chamber levels, and water moved as the gravity flow valves open.

procedure.title: Change Speed and View
procedure.description: Adjust the simulation speed and use the interactive 3D view to inspect the lock mechanism from different angles.

observation: Water flows by gravity from higher to lower elevation chambers. The ship is safely lifted by buoyancy as water fills its current lock chamber.

quiz.question: How is water moved between the locks in the Panamá Canal?
quiz.explanation: The canal relies entirely on gravity flow valves to move water between chambers.

quiz.question: What physics principle allows the ship to be lifted within the lock?
quiz.explanation: As the water level rises in the chamber, buoyancy lifts the floating ship along with the water.

title: Reverse an Array: In-Place Swap
summary: Master the Two-Pointer technique to reverse an array in-place with O(1) auxiliary space.
theory: Reversing an array or string in-place is a fundamental computer science concept. By using a Left and Right pointer and swapping elements directly, we achieve **O(1) auxiliary space** (no extra memory allocated) and **O(N) time complexity** (linear time).

procedure.title: Initialize Pointers
procedure.description: Drop two markers on the track: L at the first block, R at the last block.

procedure.title: Swap in Place
procedure.description: Swap the block at L with the block at R without allocating a new array.

procedure.title: Move Markers Inward
procedure.description: Slide marker L one step right and marker R one step left, until they meet or cross.

observation: For an 11-letter word, only 5 swaps are needed! Using two pointers is extremely memory efficient compared to creating a duplicate string.

quiz.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of reversing a string in-place using two pointers?
quiz.explanation: We only need memory for two variables (L and R) regardless of the string's length, meaning it requires O(1) constant auxiliary space.

title: Reverse a String: Out-of-Place
summary: Understand why reversing immutable strings requires O(N) extra memory space.
theory: In many programming languages, strings are **immutable**, meaning their characters cannot be modified in-place. To reverse a string without converting it to an array, we must create a completely new string in memory and build it character by character from the end of the original string. This approach results in **O(N) auxiliary space** because we allocate new memory proportional to the string's length.

procedure.title: Allocate New String
procedure.description: Observe how a brand new empty string must be created in memory.

procedure.title: Iterate Backwards
procedure.description: Watch a pointer start at the end of the original string and move backwards.

procedure.title: Concatenate
procedure.description: See each character get appended to the new string, allocating more memory space each time.

observation: Reversing an 11-letter string this way allocates 11 new character slots in memory. Compare this to the Array version, which required 0 extra slots!

quiz.question: Why does reversing an immutable string require O(N) auxiliary space?

options.text: Because it takes N operations to reverse.
Because you must create a new string of length N in memory.
Because strings take up more memory than arrays.
It doesn't, it takes O(1) space.

quiz.explanation: Since the original string cannot be modified, a new string of size N must be built, consuming O(N) extra memory.

title: Palindrome Checker: Two-Pointer Convergence
summary: Use two converging pointers to verify if a string is a palindrome in O(N) time and O(1) space.
theory: A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards (e.g., 'racecar'). The most efficient way to check for a palindrome is using the Two-Pointer technique. We place a pointer at the start (L) and end (R) of the string. We compare the characters at these pointers. If they match, we move the pointers inward. If they don't match, it is not a palindrome. We repeat this until the pointers meet in the middle.

procedure.title: Initialize Pointers
procedure.description: Place L at the first character and R at the last character.

procedure.title: Compare Characters
procedure.description: Check if the character at L is identical to the character at R.

procedure.title: Converge
procedure.description: If they match, move L right by 1 and R left by 1. Stop if they don't match.

observation: Notice how the pointers act as a mirror, checking symmetry from the outside in.

quiz.question: What happens the moment the characters at L and R do NOT match?

options.text: The loop continues until they meet.
The function immediately returns False (it is not a palindrome).
The pointers jump back to the start.

quiz.explanation: A single mismatch proves the word is not perfectly symmetrical, so we can stop checking immediately.

title: What is an Algorithm?
summary: Discover what an algorithm is by commanding a warehouse robot through a sequence of instructions to deliver a package.
theory: An algorithm is a finite, ordered sequence of well-defined instructions used to solve a specific problem. Every algorithm must have: Input (the problem data), Output (the desired result), Definiteness (every step is precisely defined), Finiteness (it terminates after finite steps), and Effectiveness (every step can be carried out). In this experiment, a robot follows instructions to pick up and deliver a package in a warehouse — demonstrating sequential execution, correctness, and why instruction order matters.

procedure.title: Observe the Algorithm
procedure.description: Read the instruction queue and predict whether the robot will successfully deliver the package.

procedure.title: Execute Step by Step
procedure.description: Use the Step Forward button to execute one instruction at a time. Watch the robot move, turn, pick up, and drop the package.

procedure.title: Try the Wrong Algorithm
procedure.description: Load the 'Wrong Instructions' algorithm and observe what happens when the instruction order is incorrect.

procedure.title: Build Your Own
procedure.description: Use the Interactive Playground to arrange your own instruction blocks and test if your algorithm delivers the package.

observation: The correct algorithm delivers the package in 6 steps with 3 moves, 1 turn, 1 pick, and 1 drop. The wrong algorithm causes a wall collision because the robot turns too early. This demonstrates that algorithms must have correct instruction order to produce the desired output.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a required property of an algorithm?
quiz.explanation: Randomness is not a required property. Algorithms must be finite, definite, and effective.

quiz.question: Why did the incorrect algorithm fail?

options.text: The instructions were in the wrong order

quiz.explanation: The wrong instruction order caused the robot to collide with a wall before reaching the package.

title: Algorithm Logic Flow
description: Observe how an algorithm makes decisions and processes logic using Sequence, Selection, and Iteration.
summary: Watch a 3D flowchart simulation execute a logical algorithm, visualizing inputs, decisions, processes, and outputs.
theory: An algorithm solves a problem using three basic constructs: Sequence, Selection, and Iteration. 1. Sequence: Executing steps in order. 2. Selection: Making decisions (e.g., IF temperature > 30 THEN Fan ON). 3. Iteration: Repeating actions in a loop.

procedure.title: Start Execution
procedure.description: Press Play to watch the robot traverse the flowchart nodes.

procedure.title: Step-by-Step
procedure.description: Use the Step button to manually advance the logic and observe the changes in Variables.

procedure.title: Advanced Mode
procedure.description: Toggle Advanced Mode to view live memory states (Temperature, Fan Relay).

observation: Instead of following a single straight line, an algorithm makes intelligent choices using Conditions. It receives input, checks logic, and modifies its output accordingly.

quiz.question: Which part of an algorithm makes a decision?
quiz.explanation: Selection (like IF/THEN) allows an algorithm to make a decision and change its path.

quiz.question: Which loop continues until a condition becomes false?
quiz.explanation: A While loop repeats continuously as long as its given condition remains true.

title: Flowcharts: Visualizing Algorithms
summary: Learn how to represent algorithms visually using standard flowchart symbols by simulating a smart traffic light controller.
theory: A flowchart is a visual representation of an algorithm. It uses standard shapes to denote different types of steps, and arrows to connect them, showing the flow of execution. Ovals represent Start/End. Rectangles represent Processes or Actions. Diamonds represent Decisions (Yes/No). Parallelograms represent Input/Output. Flowcharts make complex logic easy to understand and debug before writing any code.

procedure.title: Identify Symbols
procedure.description: Review the Flowchart Legend to understand what each shape represents.

procedure.title: Trace the Logic
procedure.description: Press Step to watch the execution indicator traverse the flowchart and see how the Traffic Light responds.

procedure.title: Observe Decisions
procedure.description: Watch the execution branch at the Decision Diamond based on the Timer condition.

observation: The execution always starts at the START node. The Decision diamond acts as a fork in the road, choosing a path based on the timer condition. The loop arrow returns execution to an earlier step, demonstrating iteration.

quiz.question: Which flowchart symbol represents a decision?
quiz.explanation: The diamond shape is universally used in flowcharts to represent a decision point, typically leading to a Yes/No branch.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the Oval symbol in a flowchart?

options.text: To indicate the Start and End of the algorithm

quiz.explanation: Ovals (terminators) are used exclusively to mark the absolute starting and ending points of a flowchart.

quiz.question: What happens when a flowchart reaches an arrow that points backwards to a previous step?

options.text: It creates a loop, repeating a section of the algorithm
It asks the user for input

quiz.explanation: Arrows that point back to earlier steps create Iteration (loops), allowing an algorithm to repeat tasks until a condition is met.
